term: wrongful termination in violation of public policy
definition: Wrongful discharge in violation of public policy (WDVPP) refers to a situation in which an employee is fired for reasons that oppose public policy interests. Such interests included protecting the individual’s rights or the general well-being of the community. An action for wrongful termination (or discharge) in violation of public policy gives a terminated employee the right to action against their former employer for wrongful termination. Although employment relationships are generally at-will, and therefore, may be terminated by either party without cause, or justifiable reason, WDVPP serves as a narrow exception to the at-will principle. This exception exists when public policy interests outweigh the need to uphold the employment contract’s terms. To make a claim for wrongful discharge in violation of public policy, a plaintiff (the terminated former employee) must show that: 1. Clear public policy existed and was manifested in some form of government law/regulation (i.e. state or federal constitution, statute or administrative regulation, or in common law); 2. Dismissing employees under such circumstances as the plaintiff's dismissal would jeopardize public policy; 3. The plaintiff's dismissal was motivated by conduct related to public policy; and 4. The employer lacked overriding legitimate business justification for the dismissal. There are four common categories in which employees may generally assert a WDVPP claim after being terminated:  Exercising a statutory right;  For example, an employee is fired for filing a worker’s compensation claim.  Refusing to do commit illegal or unlawful acts;  For example, an employee is fired for refusing to commit fraud on behalf of their employer.  Fulfilling a public obligation;  For example, an employee is fired for missing work to vote in a national election.  Whistleblowing, or reporting illegal conduct;  For example, an employee is fired for reporting their employer for using hazardous materials in their production of household products.
